seoTitle: Kona cruise port guide: tender to Kailua Pier, Aliʻi Drive
seoDescription: Kona is a tender port: boats land at Kailua Pier on Aliʻi Drive. Huliheʻe Palace $16 (Wed–Sat), free Hele-On bus, Kahaluʻu snorkelling 5 miles south (2026).
quickAnswer: Kailua-Kona is a tender port: ships anchor in Kailua Bay and tenders land at Kailua Pier, at the north end of Aliʻi Drive. Historic Kailua Village starts at the pier, so you can walk to Huliheʻe Palace and Mokuʻaikaua Church in a few minutes for free. Be back at the pier 90 minutes before all-aboard to allow for the tender queue.
intro: Kona is a port where the town is the pier. Tenders tie up at Kailua Pier, right where Aliʻi Drive begins, and the royal palace, Hawaiʻi's first Christian church and Kamehameha I's last residence are all within sight of the landing. The rest of the day depends on the sea: Kahaluʻu for snorkelling with turtles, Magic Sands for a swim if the shorebreak allows, or Puʻuhonua o Hōnaunau for a longer trip south. Everything hinges on the tender, so plan around the return queue, not the sailing time.
tenderNotes: Cruise ships anchor in Kailua Bay and tender passengers to Kailua Pier; the pier itself can only take very small vessels alongside. Tenders land at the pier at the three-way corner of Aliʻi Drive, Kaʻahumanu Place and Palani Road. Federal law sets a 100-yard security zone around each large passenger ship in the area. When the 4,000-plus-passenger Ovation of the Seas called in 2019, the state added a temporary second secure area at the end of the pier so more tenders could unload at once; the average ship calling at Kona carries 2,500 passengers or fewer. Tender operations depend on sea conditions, so check the daily programme for the last tender time.

terminals.name: Kailua Pier (tender landing)
terminals.notes: Tender landing at the north end of Aliʻi Drive. Destination Kona Coast volunteers staff the pier on every cruise day. The Hele-On Kona Trolley (Route 201) serves the pier. Taxis wait near the pier.

walkability.detail: Huliheʻe Palace, Mokuʻaikaua Church, Ahuʻena Heiau, Kamakahonu beach and the Kona Farmers Market are all along the first few hundred metres of Aliʻi Drive from the pier, on a flat seafront road. The beaches south of town (Magic Sands about 4 miles, Kahaluʻu about 5 miles) need a ride.

transportSections.time: A few minutes to Huliheʻe Palace and Mokuʻaikaua Church
transportSections.detail: Walk south from the pier along Aliʻi Drive and the seawall. Kamakahonu (King Kam) beach and Ahuʻena Heiau are right beside the pier.

transportSections.mode: Hele-On Kona Trolley (Route 201, Aliʻi Drive circulator)
transportSections.cost: Free (Hele-On fare-free extended in December 2025 for three years; 2026)
transportSections.time: Limited trips per day; check the current timetable
transportSections.detail: Route 201 serves Kailua Pier and runs south along Aliʻi Drive towards Magic Sands and Kahaluʻu. Service runs seven days a week, but trips are infrequent, so read the West Hawaiʻi timetable on the Hele-On website before relying on it for the return.

transportSections.cost: Fare not verified; confirm before you set off
transportSections.time: Depends on traffic on Aliʻi Drive
transportSections.detail: Taxis wait near the pier. Use a taxi for Kahaluʻu or Magic Sands if the trolley timing does not fit, and arrange the return before you go.

transportSections.time: Needed for Puʻuhonua o Hōnaunau (about 23.5 miles south)
transportSections.detail: Several rental offices are near the pier. The National Park Service warns that travel times vary with traffic in North Kona. Paid lots line the waterfront, and there is a free county lot one block up between Kuakini Highway and Likana Lane.

returnTiming.rule: Be at Kailua Pier for the tender 90 minutes before all-aboard. Leave Kahaluʻu or Magic Sands at least 2 hours before all-aboard, and Puʻuhonua o Hōnaunau at least 3 hours before.
returnTiming.detail: Everyone returns at once in the last two hours, and the tender queue sets your real deadline, not the sailing time. The Kona Trolley runs only a few trips a day, so do not plan a return around its last run. Roads along Aliʻi Drive and Kuakini Highway close for events such as the Ironman World Championship in October and the monthly Kokua Kailua Village Stroll.
returnTiming.emergencyFallback: From the beaches south of town, take a taxi straight to Kailua Pier. If you will miss the last tender, call the port agent number on your daily programme immediately; the cruise line representative usually waits at the pier while the ship is at anchor.

excursionAdvice: Skip the ship tour for the village: the palace, church and heiau are a few minutes' walk from the tender landing. Kahaluʻu is easy on your own if you hire snorkel gear across the road and keep an eye on the clock. A ship tour is worth it for Puʻuhonua o Hōnaunau, coffee farms upslope or anything further, such as volcano country, because one slow drive back can mean missing the last tender.

dayPlan.intro: Assumes the ship anchors at 07:00, first tenders ashore around 08:00, and all-aboard is 17:00 for a 17:30 sailing, on a Wednesday to Saturday when Huliheʻe Palace is open.

steps.what: Tender ashore at Kailua Pier. Look at Ahuʻena Heiau across the little beach at Kamakahonu, then walk south on Aliʻi Drive.
Breakfast and Kona coffee at Island Lava Java on Aliʻi Drive.
Catch the Kona Trolley or a taxi south to Kahaluʻu Beach Park. Rent snorkel gear across the road if you need it.
Snorkel at Kahaluʻu while the lifeguards are on duty (from 09:30). Float, do not stand on the coral, and give turtles space.
Ride back towards the village. Lunch of poke, for example at Da Poke Shack on the way.
Huliheʻe Palace, self-guided (last entry 14:30). Mokuʻaikaua Church is across the road.
Browse the Kona Farmers Market at Aliʻi Drive and Hualālai Road for coffee and fruit. Bring cash.
Swim or sit at Kamakahonu beach beside the pier.
Join the tender queue at Kailua Pier, 90 minutes before all-aboard.

sights.name: Huliheʻe Palace
sights.why: Royal summer house built in 1838, now a museum of koa furniture and objects from the reigns of King Kalākaua and Queen Kapiʻolani, run by the Daughters of Hawaiʻi.
sights.cost: $16 adult, $14 age 6–17 (non-resident, self-guided); guided Moʻolelo tour $20 (2026)
sights.tip: Open Wednesday to Saturday only, 10:00–15:00, last entry 14:30. Booking online is encouraged; guided tours need a reservation.

sights.name: Mokuʻaikaua Church
sights.why: Hawaiʻi's earliest Christian church, founded in 1820; the present stone building dates from about 1835–37, partly built with stones from a nearby heiau.
sights.tip: The sanctuary reopened in November 2025; visiting hours are Sundays 10:00–12:00 and Wednesdays 10:00–13:00. Outside those times you can see the exterior across from the palace.

sights.name: Ahuʻena Heiau and Kamakahonu
sights.why: The restored temple platform at the last royal residence of Kamehameha I, beside the tender landing.
sights.tip: View it from the pier and the beach. Stay off the heiau platform.

sights.name: Aliʻi Drive seafront
sights.why: The village's main street runs along the seawall from the pier past the palace, shops and cafés.
sights.tip: On Kokua Kailua Village Stroll days the street is car-free from 13:00 to 18:00.

sights.name: Kona Farmers Market
sights.why: Stalls of crafts, flowers, Kona coffee and tropical fruit at Aliʻi Drive and Hualālai Road.
sights.tip: Open Wednesday to Sunday, 07:00–16:00. Most vendors prefer cash.

sights.name: Kahaluʻu Beach Park
sights.why: Sheltered bay about 5 miles south known for calm snorkelling and green sea turtles, with lifeguards and an education centre.
sights.cost: Free entry; snorkel rental $18 a day across the road (2026)
sights.tip: Lifeguards on duty 09:30–16:45. Do not swim past the second lifeguard tower, where the surf zone starts. The beach can open late on the first Thursday of the month and closes occasionally during coral spawning.

sights.name: Puʻuhonua o Hōnaunau National Historical Park
sights.why: A place of refuge with reconstructed temple and royal grounds on the coast south of Kona.
sights.cost: $20 per private vehicle or $10 per person walk-in; card only, no cash (2026)
sights.tip: About 20 miles south on Highway 11 then 3.5 miles on Highway 160. Only for long calls; take the ship tour if your all-aboard is early.

beaches.name: Kamakahonu (King Kam Beach)
beaches.howToGetThere: Walk; it is right beside Kailua Pier
beaches.note: Small, calm beach by the tender landing with a beach shack renting gear. Keep children close near the pier.

beaches.name: Magic Sands (Laʻaloa Beach Park)
beaches.howToGetThere: Kona Trolley or taxi south on Aliʻi Drive
beaches.note: Strong shorebreak onto a shallow bottom, and the sand comes and goes with the surf. Lifeguards on duty 09:30–16:45; ask them before swimming.

beaches.name: Kahaluʻu Beach Park
beaches.howToGetThere: Kona Trolley or taxi south on Aliʻi Drive
beaches.cost: Free; visitor parking $12 for four hours if driving (2026)
beaches.note: The best snorkelling close to town. The lava-rock entry is slippery; a current sets north and out to sea in big swell.

beaches.name: Honl's Beach
beaches.note: Small and rocky at the waterline; water shoes help.

commonMistakes.mistake: Planning Huliheʻe Palace on a Sunday, Monday or Tuesday.
commonMistakes.fix: The palace opens Wednesday to Saturday only, 10:00–15:00 with last entry at 14:30. Check your port day.

commonMistakes.mistake: Returning to the pier 30 minutes before all-aboard.
commonMistakes.fix: Join the tender queue 90 minutes before. Every passenger returns in the same window.

commonMistakes.mistake: Standing on coral or touching turtles and manta rays.
commonMistakes.fix: Float over the reef, give turtles space and never touch mantas; state fines for touching manta rays start at $500.
Hawaiʻi banned sunscreens with oxybenzone and octinoxate in 2021. Use a mineral one (zinc oxide or titanium dioxide); Kahaluʻu has free dispensers at the pavilion 09:00–15:00.

commonMistakes.mistake: Driving to Puʻuhonua o Hōnaunau on a short call or carrying only cash.
commonMistakes.fix: Allow 4–5 hours and leave the park 3 hours before all-aboard. The park takes cards only.

safety: Kailua-Kona is a calm, low-crime town for visitors. The real risks are in the water and the sun. Swim at lifeguarded beaches (Magic Sands and Kahaluʻu are staffed 09:30–16:45), read the hazard signs and check hioceansafety.com for surf conditions. Magic Sands has a hard shorebreak, and Kahaluʻu has a current that can strengthen in big swell. Lava rock is sharp and slippery, so wear water shoes. Volcanic haze (vog) can affect people with asthma; check the air-quality forecast. Mornings are usually clearest; clouds build after midday.
scams: Timeshare activity booths: booths offering cheap or free tours in return for attending a timeshare sales presentation operate in Hawaiʻi. State law (HRS §514E-11) requires such booths to display a permanent 'time share' sign and agents to disclose that the offer is a sales inducement. On a port day, a presentation will eat hours you do not have.
accessibility: The tender landing, Kailua Pier and the area around it are reported to be wheelchair accessible, with ramps and accessible parking. Tender boarding depends on the swell, so ask the ship whether wheelchair users can transfer on the day. Aliʻi Drive is flat along the seafront. Huliheʻe Palace is a 19th-century building with stairs; the palace can make alternative arrangements if you call (808) 595-6291 at least 48 hours ahead. At Kahaluʻu, visitors with disabilities can get a free parking pass from the attendant, but the beach entry is uneven lava rock.
rainyDay: Kona's showers usually come in the afternoon. Visit Huliheʻe Palace (Wednesday to Saturday) and Mokuʻaikaua Church if it is open, then shelter in cafés along Aliʻi Drive or the Kona Brewing pub. Skip snorkelling if heavy rain has made the water murky or the surf is up, and ask the lifeguards before going in.
crowdTips: Most days bring one ship, but a single large ship can land more than 4,000 people through one small pier. Get on an early tender, go straight to Kahaluʻu while it is quiet and lifeguarded, and see the village in the early afternoon. Huliheʻe Palace limits guided tours, so book ahead. Avoid big event days such as the Ironman World Championship in October, when roads around the village close.

faqs.a: Yes. Cruise ships anchor in Kailua Bay and tender passengers to Kailua Pier at the start of Aliʻi Drive.

faqs.q: Is Kailua-Kona walkable from the cruise port?
faqs.a: Yes. The tenders land in the village; Huliheʻe Palace, Mokuʻaikaua Church and the farmers market are a few minutes' walk along Aliʻi Drive.

faqs.q: How do I get from Kona cruise port to Kahaluʻu Beach?
faqs.a: Take the free Hele-On Kona Trolley (Route 201) or a taxi about 5 miles south along Aliʻi Drive. Check the trolley timetable first, as trips are limited.

faqs.q: Is the Hele-On bus free in Kona?
faqs.a: Yes. Hele-On is fare-free; in December 2025 the county extended free fares for three more years.

faqs.q: What can I do in Kona in one day from a cruise ship?
faqs.a: Snorkel with turtles at Kahaluʻu in the morning, then walk the village: Huliheʻe Palace, Mokuʻaikaua Church, Ahuʻena Heiau and the farmers market.
Kamakahonu is beside the pier. Honl's is about a mile south, Magic Sands about 4 miles and Kahaluʻu about 5 miles.

faqs.q: Can I visit Puʻuhonua o Hōnaunau from a cruise ship in Kona?
faqs.a: On a long call, by rental car or ship tour. It is about 23.5 miles south; entry is $20 per car or $10 per person, card only (2026).
Yes for visitors. Take care in the ocean: swim at lifeguarded beaches and respect the shorebreak and currents.
